extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of logic, philosophy of science, and scientific method
extracted.subtask_description: Principles and standards for inductive reasoning, the law of causation, classification, and the justification of scientific inference across the sciences. Focuses on what induction can legitimately establish and how to evaluate generalizations, probabilities, and conceptual definitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of uniformity required for induction
rubrics_metrics.description: Generalizations do not imply that there was uniformity in every thing, but only that as much uniformity as existed within their observation, existed also beyond it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The induction 'fire burns' requires only uniformity in that particular class of natural phenomena (effects of fire on senses and combustibles); induction does not presuppose a principle of universal uniformity anterior to experience — the uniformity required is proved by the experience itself.

rubrics_metrics.name: Law of causation as an inductive conclusion (not a priori)
rubrics_metrics.description: The law of causation is not known a priori; it is itself a conclusion from experience rather than an independent presupposed truth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid treating causation as an innate, intuitive certainty; recognize that asserted universal causal laws should be justified by observed uniform sequences and verified instances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abstraction cannot establish universality beyond experience
rubrics_metrics.description: Abstract conceptions elicited from experience cannot be evidence of an objective fact in universal Nature beyond what the experience itself bears witness of.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not infer that mere abstract analysis or faculty of abstraction provides assurance of universality that observation does not; abstraction may analyze but cannot extend empirical warrant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scientific conclusions are conditionally certain
rubrics_metrics.description: When physical science is said to depend on the assumption that the course of nature is invariable, the conclusions of physical science are not absolute truths but conditional on the uniformity of the course of nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat scientific results as true 'if, and as long as, the present laws of nature are valid' — this conditional conclusiveness is sufficient for guiding conduct, though not metaphysical certainty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical sufficiency of high probability
rubrics_metrics.description: Even without perfect certitude, a very high degree of probability can justify acting upon a presumption until an exception appears.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use examples (e.g., opened chambers all dodecahedral) to justify that well-confirmed uniformities grant a practical presumption of universality for decision and action, though not absolute proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constitutive basis for believing in general uniformity
rubrics_metrics.description: The uniformity of the course of nature as a whole is constituted by the uniform sequences of special effects from special natural agencies; these agencies are not incalculably numerous in the part known to us, and many have been made amenable to observation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argue for global uniformity by assembling evidence of fixed laws of many natural agencies and their combinations — this observed scope supports assurance of uniformity comparable to that of best-known phenomena.

rubrics_metrics.name: Miracles interpreted as new antecedent causes, not breaches of causation
rubrics_metrics.description: In every case of alleged miracle, a new antecedent is affirmed to exist; a counteracting cause — the volition of a supernatural being; therefore miracles are cases of the Law of Universal Causation, not deviations from it, for those who accept supernatural volitions as vera causa.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating alleged exceptions to natural law, distinguish between genuine suspension of causal laws and claims that posit new causal agents; the latter do not falsify causation but change antecedent conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Justification of inductive inference about the future
rubrics_metrics.description: Though we have had no experience of what is future, we have had abundant experience of what was future; the proof follows presumption by subsequent verification when the future becomes present and observable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat the inductive 'leap' to future events as analogous to inference about unobserved pasts — presumption is psychologically immediate but is validated by later observation; this supports inductive expectation of conformity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interdependence of uniformity and causation
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no other uniformity in the events of nature than that which arises from the law of causation; if uniformity of course of nature has exceptions, to that extent the law of causation fails.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate claims of non-causal events cautiously since admitting events without causes undermines the universality of causal explanation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identification of natural Kinds by conjunction of properties
rubrics_metrics.description: Most commonly several properties are required to identify a Kind; each property considered singly is a joint property of that and other Kinds, but together they identify its Kind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In classification, avoid identifying kinds by a single characteristic when it is shared with others; use conjunctions of multiple ascertained properties (including those still unascertained) to mark a class.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicability of general canons of induction to special sciences
rubrics_metrics.description: Canons of Induction as laid down in general logic are applicable to chemistry and other sciences; special adaptations required by inductive methods in particular sciences belong to the logic of the special sciences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply general inductive principles across disciplines, but allow domain-specific methodological adaptations to be developed by those treating the logic of the special sciences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit on inferences from approximate generalizations
rubrics_metrics.description: From premises like 'Most A are B' and 'Most A are C' we may infer with certainty only that some B are C; this is the utmost limit when the precise degree of approximation is unknown.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not overreach from two approximate generalizations to strong universal conclusions; quantify and clarify degrees of approximation if stronger inferences are to be attempted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Correct evaluation of combined probabilities via causal analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: The degree of frequency of a coincidence depends on, and is a measure of, the frequency combined with the efficacy of the causes in operation that are favorable to it; probabilistic evaluation should analyze the causes operating on each class rather than naïvely combining marginal frequencies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When computing joint probabilities (e.g., proportion of As that are Bs and Cs), reason from the causal operations and their joint efficacy rather than applying incorrect combinatorial shortcuts; work through case analysis when causes operate jointly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of impossibility tied to complete induction
rubrics_metrics.description: An impossibility is that, the truth of which would conflict with a complete induction, that is, with the most conclusive evidence which we possess of universal truth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish genuine impossibilities (those incompatible with complete induction) from things merely currently unexplained or improbable due to ignorance — many supposed impossibilities may be overturned by future causal discovery (e.g., high-speed travel, painless operations).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer concept definitions that capture the essential attribute (example: parallels as equidistant)
rubrics_metrics.description: Defining parallel lines by being in the same plane and never meeting necessitates extra axioms; equidistance is a fitter property to characterize parallels since it captures the attribute really involved in the signification of the name.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When defining mathematical or conceptual terms, choose properties that express the essence of the concept (avoid definitions that force additional unrelated axioms); ensure definitions align with intuitive and functional meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid inappropriate conceptions in explanation and generalization
rubrics_metrics.description: Applying inappropriate conceptions (not merely less-fit ones) — e.g., forcing a geometrical conception of circular properties to explain mechanical relations — leads to false explanations when the conception has no prototype in nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critically examine whether the abstract conception applied to explain a phenomenon has an actual counterpart in facts; avoid resolving laws of nature into more general laws that are imaginary or irrelevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize and avoid common logical fallacies of generalization
rubrics_metrics.description: Fallacies such as à dicto secundum quid ad dictum simpliciter (illicit generalization) and its converse (fallacia accidentis) arise when one improperly moves between qualified and unqualified propositions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be alert to the direction of generalization and qualification in arguments (e.g., do not infer an unqualified universal from a qualified statement or vice versa); consult examples of both fallacies to diagnose reasoning errors.
